analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum federal standards for sports betting, with deposit limits, ad restrictions, and gambling-addiction safeguards.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with no cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban sports betting nationwide except in states whose programs apply to and win approval from the Attorney General under a set of federal minimum standards. Those standards include banning credit-card deposits, capping deposits at five per day, affordability checks before large wagers, a national self-exclusion list for people trying to quit, restrictions on gambling ads, a ban on proposition bets on college sports, and rules against using artificial intelligence to target individual bettors. It would also fund national surveys and surveillance of gambling addiction.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports and their families, especially problem gamblers and young bettors. The bill would stop operators from taking credit-card deposits, limit how often someone can deposit money in a day, require an income check before bets above $1,000 in a day or $10,000 in a month, and let a person put themselves on a national list that bars all licensed sportsbooks from taking their wagers [S2]. It would also ban ads during live games and most daytime TV, ban 'bonus bet' style promotions, prohibit proposition bets on college and amateur sports, and stop operators from using AI to tailor offers to individual bettors [S2]. Public health agencies would get new nationwide data on problem gambling [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sports bettors, problem gamblers, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Bars operators from accepting deposits made with a credit card and limits bettors to five deposits in a 24-hour period, with affordability checks before deposits exceed $1,000 in a day or $10,000 in 30 days [S2].

Creates a national self-exclusion list, so a person who wants to stop gambling can block themselves from every licensed sportsbook in participating states, plus a state-level process with wager limits [S2].

Restricts advertising: no ads between 8am and 10pm local time or during live game broadcasts, no 'bonus', 'no sweat', or 'bonus bet' promotions, and no ads targeting problem gamblers or people under 21 [S2].

Prohibits operators from using artificial intelligence to track an individual's bets, target them with offers, or create gambling products such as microbets, and bans proposition bets on amateur and intercollegiate sports [S2].

Requires annual federal surveys of online betting harms, a Surgeon General's report on sports betting's public health challenges, and a CDC-run National Gambling Addiction Surveillance System, with surveys that cannot be conducted or funded by the gambling industry [S2].

Prohibits wagering on sporting events after they have started and bars athletes, coaches, officials, and credentialed insiders from betting on their own sports, with suspicious-transaction reporting to regulators, leagues, and law enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Sports betting operators, the companies running online and retail sportsbooks. They would face compliance costs, lose credit-card-funded deposits and high-frequency deposit patterns, lose targeted AI marketing and microbet products, and pay a share of revenue into gambling-disorder treatment and education [S2]. States with existing programs would have to apply for federal approval and meet the standards or their markets would become unlawful [S2]. Recreational bettors would face more friction, such as deposit caps and income verification for larger bets [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Sports betting operators and some frequent bettors

drawbacks.text: Federalizing the rules would override the state-by-state regulatory systems most states have already built, forcing all existing programs to reapply to the Attorney General under a new federal framework, which states and operators would resist as duplicative bureaucracy [S2].

Heavier friction for legal bettors, such as deposit caps, income checks, and ad bans, could push some wagering toward unregulated offshore sites that have none of these protections, a common objection to strict gambling restrictions [S2].

The bill leaves legal sports betting in place as a permanent industry under a federal licensing framework; it regulates the market rather than ending it, and operators keep a government-approved channel to their customers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and public-health protections are real and targeted at the fastest-growing part of gambling: an industry that can now take unlimited deposits from a phone. The strongest honest objection is design, not principle: imposing a single federal approval process on dozens of functioning state systems adds bureaucracy, and tighter friction on legal betting may move some volume to offshore books with zero safeguards. On balance, the protections for problem gamblers outweigh the compliance costs, but the federal override of state programs is a genuine trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the SAFE Bet Act in the House on September 12, 2024 [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S4].
No other member of the House, from either party, signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without a committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sports betting operators are better off: they continue operating under the existing patchwork of state rules, with no federal affordability checks, no national self-exclusion list, and no restrictions on credit-card deposits, betting ads, or AI-targeted promotions. Bettors and their families get none of the bill's protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sports betting operators, who keep the status quo

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees; recruited no cosponsors before the session ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 12, 2024 and took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sports betting industry
against.what_they_did: The bill's strict federal standards, ad bans, and restrictions on betting products drew opposition from an industry that benefits from the existing state-by-state regime; it publicly lobbied against federal restrictions of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, and not a single member of either party cosponsored the bill; its only supporter was its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would lock legal sports betting in as a permanent, federally licensed industry while imposing heavy rules on it: credit-card deposit bans, deposit and affordability limits, ad restrictions, bans on AI targeting and microbets, and a revenue share for addiction treatment. Operators profit from encouraging wagering volume, so their interest runs against the bettor protections in the bill.

Leagues would get the power to request restrictions on wagers to protect contest integrity, receive suspicious-transaction reports, and control licensed data used to settle bets. These powers align with fans' interest in clean games, though they also formalize league control over betting data.
The bill bans funding betting deposits with credit cards, cutting off an interchange revenue stream tied to borrowed-money gambling.

The bill deems an online wager to occur where the betting server sits, which can place wagers on Indian lands when a tribal-state compact exists, potentially benefiting tribal operators, but tribes would also have to fit into the new federal approval framework.
